# Grief and end-of-life counseling

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Preoperative and postoperative care > Grief and end-of-life counseling*

[Original Article Link](/library/jH0_Jh)

---

## Summary

<u>Bereavement</u> is the loss of a close relation or friend to <u>death</u>. <u>Grief</u> is the internal experience of sadness in response to <u>bereavement</u>, and it is expressed through culturally and socially influenced practices of <u>mourning</u>. <u>Grief</u> can also be experienced by dying individuals themselves and those close to them in anticipation of <u>death</u>. Individual reactions to <u>grief</u> are determined by factors such as <u>personality</u>, psychiatric history, and access to support systems. <u>Normal grief</u> is characterized by psychiatric symptoms (e.g., intense sorrow, <u>anxiety</u>, guilt, emotional <u>distress</u>) and somatic symptoms (e.g., nonspecific <u>chest pain</u>, <u>headaches</u>) lasting 6–12 months. <u>Persistent complex bereavement disorder</u> is a psychiatric condition characterized by <u>grief</u> and/or <u>mourning</u> that lasts for at least 12 months and results in severe <u>distress</u> and functional impairment. Practitioners use the <u>SPIKES protocol</u>, a set of guidelines for <u>breaking bad news</u> to terminally ill patients. End-of-life counseling is a <u>patient-centered approach</u> that addresses the dying person's practical, psychological, emotional, and spiritual care needs. <u>Bereavement</u> counseling provides emotional support to the family and caregivers while screening for psychiatric illness caused by <u>stress</u> (e.g., <u>persistent complex bereavement disorder</u>). Caring for dying patients can be emotionally and psychologically demanding. Physicians should be attentive to their own <u>grief</u> following the <u>death</u> of a patient and seek support from colleagues.

---

## Definitions

* Bereavement: the loss of a close relation or friend to <u>death</u>

* <u>Grief</u>: the internal experience of sadness in response to <u>bereavement</u> and other meaningful losses (e.g., loss of functional abilities)

* Mourning: the outward expression of <u>grief</u> as influenced by factors such as religious beliefs, social norms, and cultural traditions

## Bereavement and grief

### <u>Bereavement</u> [[2]](/library/14c2Rc0)




* Reactions to <u>death</u> can be influenced by factors such as <u>personality</u>, psychiatric history, access to support systems, and the nature of the relationship to the deceased.

* <u>Stress</u> caused by <u>bereavement</u> can have a negative impact on health.

* Can precipitate or worsen physical/somatic illnesses (e.g., <u>MI</u>, <u>stress-induced cardiomyopathy</u>) and psychiatric disorders (e.g., <u>MDD</u>, <u>PTSD</u>, <u>insomnia</u>)

* Increased risk of unhealthy behaviors (e.g., elevated tobacco and <u>alcohol</u> consumption, poor nutrition)

* Increased risk of <u>suicidal ideation</u>





### Types of <u>grief</u> [[1]](/library/bJcHsW0)




#### Normal grief




* Characteristics

* Often occurs in waves

* Duration varies significantly (resolves within 6 to 12 months)

* Intense sorrow, yearning for the deceased, emotional <u>distress</u>

* Guilt connected to the care, loss, or prior relationship with the deceased

* <u>Anxiety</u>

* <u>Insomnia</u>

* <u>Anorexia</u>, weight loss

* Somatic symptoms (e.g., nonspecific <u>chest pain</u>, epigastric discomfort, <u>headaches</u>)

* Thoughts of preoccupation, about <u>death</u>, and memories of the deceased

* <u>Illusions</u> or <u>hallucinations</u> of the deceased (considered normal if the individual does not believe that they are real)

* No significant <u>suicidal ideation</u>

* No persistent or long-term functional impairment

* Preoccupation with thoughts and memories of the deceased and the circumstances surrounding their <u>death</u>

* Differential diagnosis

* Some symptoms are similar to those seen in <u>major depressive disorder</u> (<u>MDD</u>): Primary affects in <u>grief</u> are emptiness and loss that decrease in intensity and frequency over time, whereas <u>MDD</u> is characterized by persistent <u>depressed mood</u> with feelings of worthlessness and low self-esteem

* <u>Acute stress disorder</u>

* See “<u>Differential diagnoses of trauma- and stressor-related disorders</u>” and “Differential diagnosis” in “<u>Major depressive disorder</u>”.





##### Models of <u>normal grief</u>




* Kubler-Ross model [[3]](/library/OGcIzd0)

* A model describing 5 stages of <u>grief</u> following a loss:

* Denial

* Anger

* Bargaining

* <u>Depression</u>

* Acceptance

* Individuals may experience some or all of these stages and not always in the order presented above.

* The four phases of <u>grief</u> model [[4]](/library/lGcvzd0)

* A model describing 4 phases of <u>grief</u> following a loss:

* <u>Shock</u> or numbness

* Yearning or searching

* Disorganization or despair

* Reorganization

* Proponents of this model believe that <u>grief</u> is a waxing and waning of the emotional process instead of fixed phases.





#### Persistent complex bereavement disorder [[5]](/library/Nta-dm)




* Definition: a mental disorder characterized by an unusually prolonged period of <u>grief</u> and/or <u>mourning</u> (lasting at least 12 months in adults and 6 months in children) resulting in severe <u>distress</u> and functional impairment.

* Overview

* Diagnosis is based on five criteria.

* Criteria C and D require symptoms to have been experienced most days and persisted for at least one year

* Differential diagnosis: <u>PTSD</u>, <u>depressive disorders</u>, and <u>normal grief</u>

* Diagnostic criteria  

* Criterion A: the individual has experienced the <u>death</u> of a close relation or friend

* Criterion B

* Symptoms related to yearning, longing, and sorrow

* Requires at least one of four symptoms experienced on most days and that persisted for at least 12 months in adults or 6 months in children

* Persistent yearning and/or longing for the deceased

* Intense sorrow and <u>emotional pain</u> in response to the <u>death</u>

* Preoccupation with the deceased

* Preoccupation with the circumstances of the <u>death</u>

* Criterion C

* Symptoms of reactive <u>distress</u> to the <u>death</u>

* Marked difficulty accepting <u>death</u>

* Experiencing disbelief or emotional numbness

* Difficulty with positive reminiscing about the deceased

* Bitterness or anger related to <u>death</u>

* Maladaptive appraisals about oneself in relation to the deceased or the <u>death</u> (e.g., self-blame)

* Excessive avoidance of reminders of the loss

* Symptoms of social/identity disruption

* A desire to die in order to be with the deceased

* Feeling that life is meaningless or empty without the deceased, or the belief that one cannot function without the deceased

* Difficulty trusting other individuals since the <u>death</u>

* Feeling alone or detached from other individuals since the <u>death</u>

* Confusion about one's role in life or a diminished sense of one's identity

* Difficulty or reluctance to pursue interests since the loss or to plan for the future

* Criterion D: clinically significant <u>distress</u> or functional impairment

* Criterion E: <u>distress</u> or functional impairment that goes beyond of sociocultural norms

* Management

* <u>Psychotherapy</u>

* In case of <u>depression</u>: <u>antidepressants</u>

## End-of-life counseling

### Overview




* Definition: <u>End-of-life counseling</u> is an individualized, holistic, <u>patient-centered approach</u> that addresses the dying person's practical, psychological, emotional, and spiritual care needs (see “<u>General concepts of patient counseling</u>” in "<u>Patient communication and counseling</u>").

* Goals

* To involve the patient in end-of-life treatment decisions for improved care, comfort, and quality of life

* To provide comfort and psychosocial support for family and caregiver

* To determine the patient's wishes regarding the involvement of others (e.g., family, caregivers) in care

* To establish the patient's <u>goals of care</u>

* To inform all individuals involved in the patient's care of the patient's and family's wishes regarding end-of-life treatment including <u>palliative care</u> (See “<u>End-of-life issues</u>.”)





### SPIKES protocol [[6]](/library/VhYG1K)




The <u>SPIKES protocol</u> is a set of recommendations to help practitioners communicate bad news to patients.




| SPIKES protocol overview |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initials | Element | Description |
| S | <br>* Setting<br><br> | <br><br>* Set up the interview and arrange for privacy.<br><br>* Involve family and partners.<br><br>* Manage schedules to avoid interruptions.<br><br><br> |
| P | <br>* Perception<br><br> | <br><br>* Determine the patient's perception of the situation.<br><br>* Ask open-ended questions.<br><br>* Encourage the patient to explain their illness, therapy, and/or prognosis in their own words.<br><br><br> |
| I | <br>* Invitation<br><br> | <br><br>* Invite the patient to ask questions about their condition, prognosis, and/or treatment.<br><br>* Offer the opportunity to talk at a later date.<br><br>* Honor the patient's wishes if they do not want to know further details about their condition.<br><br><br> |
| K | <br>* Knowledge<br><br> | <br><br>* Warn the patient that you have difficult news before discussing their prognosis.<br><br>* Avoid technical terms.<br><br>* Use short and precise sentences.<br><br>* Communicate any positive information about their condition.<br><br>* Confirm that the patient understands the information you have given them.<br><br><br> |
| E | <br>* Emotions<br><br> | <br>* Identify emotional triggers and acknowledge the patient's emotions with empathic nonverbal responses.<br><br> |
| S | <br>* Summary and Strategy<br><br> | <br><br>* Summarize and strategize a plan that reflects the patient's needs and wishes.<br><br>* Asking the patient about potential solutions can help them to feel in control.<br><br><br> |





### Counseling for specific scenarios




#### Counseling for terminally ill patients




* General considerations

* Patient adjustment to the prospect of <u>death</u> is influenced by a variety of factors, including disease progression, cultural and religious beliefs, <u>coping mechanisms</u>, and available support systems.

* Patients with terminal diseases may feel isolated, frustrated, and/or hopeless.

* These patients should be counseled on <u>learning</u> how to handle difficult emotions and develop an understanding of their disease.

* <u>Counseling for terminally ill patients</u>

* Emphasize that the patient is not alone and offer referrals to support groups.

* Listen to the patient's frustrations and challenges and empathize with them; do not dismiss their concerns.

* Avoid platitudes such as “Everything will be OK” or “I'm sure you'll feel better soon.”

* <u>Discuss goals of care</u>, including <u>DNR orders</u>, with the patient and family.

* Work together with the patient to identify sources of <u>stress</u>.

* Counsel the patient on modest lifestyle changes that could improve comfort and quality of life.

* Consider that the patients' wishes may differ from those of family members (e.g., patients may have come to terms with their imminent <u>death</u>, but family members demand further treatment or refuse to accept the circumstances.).

* Assess for psychological <u>distress</u> (e.g., fear of being forgotten or abandoned, fear of the dying process, existential loneliness) [[7]](/library/uPcpgc0)

* Provide resources for coping with emotional and existential <u>distress</u> (e.g., existential <u>psychotherapy</u>, meaning-centered <u>group psychotherapy</u>). [[8]](/library/FPcggc0)

* Screen for anticipatory <u>grief</u> (e.g., increased awareness of shortened life span, perception of being disconnected from others).

* Ensure that all care providers interact with the patient in an empathic way.





##### Spiritual care and counseling in terminally ill patients




* General considerations

* Spiritual care attends to the individual spiritual and/or religious needs and beliefs of a terminally ill patient and represents an essential component of <u>palliative care</u>.

* Spiritual and/or religious patients may wish to discuss their beliefs and associated challenges with their <u>health care providers</u>.

* A <u>palliative care</u> team should be multidisciplinary, not only consisting of physicians but also psychological experts and professionals with education and training in pastoral care (e.g., spiritual assistants).

* <u>Health care professionals</u> should be trained to assess a patient's spirituality and signs of associated <u>distress</u>. [[9]](/library/ZJcZsW0)

* Screening may include prompts such as:

* “Do you consider yourself spiritual/religious?”

* “How important is religion to you?”

* “What importance does your spirituality have in your life?”

* “Does your religion/spirituality provide you all the comfort and strength you need from it right now?”,

* “How well are those resources working for you at this time?” [[10]](/library/0JcesW0)

* If the patient shows signs of spiritual <u>distress</u>, referral to a board-certified <u>chaplain</u> of their faith is advised.

* Physicians should support their patients' religious and spiritual practices, provided that they are appropriate and do not interfere with medical care.

* Failure to provide adequate spiritual support is associated with increased patient dissatisfaction, decreased use of <u>hospice care</u>, and poorer quality of life.

* Goals

* Reduction of psychosocial and spiritual <u>distress</u>

* Promotion of dignity and meaning at the end of life

* Improvement of overall quality of life through a supportive understanding of the patient's spiritual and/or religious beliefs and values





#### End-of-life counseling for families




* Assess and support family caregivers during the prebereavement period and develop pathways for <u>bereavement</u> care.

* Ensure the family members are aware and informed of the changes in the condition of the dying relative.

* Assess preparedness for <u>death</u>.

* Ask what kind of support the family desires leading up to or after the <u>death</u> of the relative.

* Answer questions in detail and address the next steps (e.g., what to expect, deterioration, loss of abilities)

* Listen and offer support, while also remaining professional

* Encourage gathering information on the illness and offer resources about the illness, <u>grief</u>, and <u>bereavement</u> services.

* In some cases, follow up with caregivers to assess how they are coping and plan a follow-up appointment.





#### Addressing family and friends after death




If family or friends are present: [[11]](/library/MZcMXa0)




* Introduce yourself (e.g., “I am Dr. X. I am one of the doctors on the team taking care of “Mr. Y” or “I am covering for the doctors taking care of Mr. Y”) and explain why you are there (e.g., “I regret to inform you that Mr. Y has died”).

* If possible, sit with the caregivers or family members.

* Be direct in disclosing the <u>death</u> and avoid any euphemisms that may be ambiguous.

* Offer condolences (e.g., “I'm so sorry for your loss”).

* Ask if they wish to be present and invite them to ask questions while you pronounce the <u>death</u>. [[12]](/library/o810ni0)

* Solicit extra help and information for families that are interested, including assisting in finding <u>psychosocial counseling</u>.

* Helpful resources include:

* Hospital <u>chaplains</u>

* Case managers and social workers

* <u>Grief</u> counselors and <u>bereavement</u> support groups

* <u>Organ donation</u> teams





#### Counseling for individuals experiencing bereavement [[13]](/library/sHXt7z)[[14]](/library/GHXB7z)




* Express sympathy and concern.

* Provide a space to discuss the patient's feelings.

* Offer resources for <u>grief</u> and <u>bereavement</u> services.

* Assess for <u>persistent complex bereavement disorder</u> and/or other mental health conditions, and refer if necessary.

* Assessment and support of family and/or caregivers during the pre-<u>bereavement</u> period and develop pathways for <u>bereavement</u> care

* Informing family members of potential changes in the condition of the dying relative

* Assessment of patient, family, and caregiver preparedness for <u>death</u>

* Assessment of the kind of support the family desires leading up to and/or after the <u>death</u> of the patient's loved ones

* Answering questions the patient may have regarding their condition and the prognosis (e.g., deterioration, loss of abilities)





#### Processing the death of a patient




* Physicians should take time to process a patient's <u>death</u>.

* Find and explore <u>coping mechanisms</u> that work for you; <u>coping strategies</u> include:

* Speaking with family, friends, and support system members.

* Reflecting on the care provided to the patient, considering in particular any positive contributions that you made.

* Sending condolences to a patient's family or loved ones if it might help to process the loss with them.

* If the <u>death</u> occurs in the middle of a busy shift and there is no time for oneself to process the loss

* Take at least a few minutes before seeing the next patient and/or take additional time after a shift to process emotions.

* Consider confiding about your emotional state with a peer, senior resident, or attending.

* Think about the ways you can help the next patient(s).

* The <u>death</u> of a patient provides an opportunity to reflect on general <u>end-of-life issues</u>.
